newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Newspaper legend Jimmy Breslin celebrates his survival.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Newspaper legend Jimmy Breslin celebrates his survival.

text.p: He has covered every sort of story from why baseball's New York Mets lost 120 games one season -- "Can't anyone here play this game?" was the phrase he made famous -- to why "Son of Sam" serial killer David Berkowitz murdered strangers.

Jimmy Breslin has drunk with the famous, visited more slums than anyone except Mother Teresa, righted wrongs, won prizes including the Pulitzer and irritated friends and foes alike. Now he has tackled one of the most complex subjects of his career -- his brain.
And he is getting rave reviews.

His account of his 1994 brain operation, "I Want to Thank My Brain for Remembering Me" (Little, Brown and Company), is not only a medical thriller but an outrageous romp through his 30 plus years as a legendary New York newspaperman.

Known as the hard-drinking champion of the working man, Breslin actually had cut down on his drinking in recent years because of diabetes. He is an avid swimmer who had never spent a night in a hospital until November 1994 when he was admitted to the Barrow Neurological Institute in Phoenix for surgery.

He had an aneurysm -- a ballooned artery wall -- in his brain and it would have killed him if it had burst. Breslin, who was 65 at the time, was advised to have Dr. Robert Spetzler of the Barrow Institute do the dangerous operation.
"He has supreme confidence," Breslin said of Spetzler. "Oh yeah, he thinks he can do anything, which is alright with me."

Spetzler successfully stapled the aneurysm and Breslin suffered no ill effects from the operation. He later returned to Phoenix for two months and watched surgeons do 20 brain operations, mostly aneurysms.

With typical lack of modesty, Breslin said he stood next to the doctors "while they're sticking their hands in the guy's head and they're telling me what they're doing. The descriptions of the medical stuff (in the book), nobody can do that. That comes from 5,000 years of covering prize fights and freakin' horse races."
Cognizant of the possibility of ending up like a vegetable should his operation fail, Breslin nevertheless had no will directing that he not be maintained on life support systems.

"I don't need any of that. We got enough intelligence and moral committment in the family to do whatever should be done at the moment it should be done, if anything went wrong," he said. "Nobody is going to keep a cucumber alive in a nursing home for 30 years or something."

Some of Breslin's detractors, of which there are many, joke that he has suffered from memory loss after the surgery. They note that while his memoir is full of anecdotes about his career it neglects to include a chapter on his suspension from New York Newsday in May 1990 for calling a Korean reporter at the paper a "yellow cur" after she sent him a note mildly criticising one of his columns.
"Jimmy Breslin has two great talents," said a former Newsday colleague. "One is for writing and the other is for lousiness. And sadly, the second surpasses even the first."

Breslin's claim in a 1988 letter to the editor of the Village Voice that he often talks nonsense and that "I am allowed to do what I want" may strike some as charming but his assertion in "I Want to Thank My Brain" that newspapers in New York "hired five people with Irish names to try to imitate me" is sure to inflame long-simmering antagonisms with the city's other tabloid columnists.

"He's one of the smartest people I ever spoke to in my life," said Jim Dwyer, the Pulitzer Prize winning columnist of the New York Daily News. "Question: When did you last speak to him? Answer: About three years ago. Question: Do you miss speaking to him? Answer: No."

Pete Hamill, another of New York's great Irish coumnists, had only kind words for Breslin. Hamill credits him with being true to his basic credo, which Hamill sums up as "comforting the afflicted and afflicting the comfortable."
"Jimmy climbed more tenament stairs in Bedford-Stuyvesant than any black columnist ever did," Hamill said.
Breslin wrote in his memoir: "I always figured that this was the only game; just go to any neighbourhood where the poor live and tell the truth about what you see."

For the first time in 20 years the man who dubbed Nancy Reagan "a country club fool" and the Ayatollah Khomeini "a desert politician" is not writing on deadline for a daily newspaper. His contract with Newsday, which has 4 1/2 years to run, stipulates that he only does columns periodically now that the paper's city edition has folded.

The columnist, who wrote that "words for a newspaper come from nervous energy on a deadline," says he does not miss the pressure. He is currently working on his sixth novel and "I better be working every day!"
